leading_positions.synthesis: All eight round-1 files give B048 (optical lattice clock; Hidetoshi Katori, Jun Ye) as the sole prize part of the preferred configuration, with the same two laureates. Shared: the magic-wavelength and Lamb-Dicke argument, independent reproduction near 1e-18 in several laboratories and species, consequences such as millimetre-scale redshift, constants and dark-matter tests and the pending redefinition of the second, and a two-name credit that most members call the cleanest on the shortlist (Katori for concept and first realisation, Ye for record accuracy and many-body clock physics). Not shared or not settled: citation wording (Danielsson, Eriksson, Lindroth, Mehlig and Olsson use 'enabling measurement of time and frequency at the 10^-18 level'; Johansson, Kroll and Pearce use wording about opening a new regime of precision), and how firm the chronology is, since all eight say they are working partly from memory or from colleagues' ballots. Several members state that they moved to B048 from a different opening first choice (Danielsson EHT, Eriksson B019, Johansson B001, Mehlig B011, Olsson B054, Pearce B033), so this is convergence in the round-1 files, not agreement in the opening rankings.

areas_of_agreement: All eight members explicitly prefer a single-part B048 configuration crediting Katori and Ye.

No file disputes the scientific mechanism: magic-wavelength trapping cancels the lattice light shift while many atoms are held in the Lamb-Dicke regime, and clocks near 1e-18 are reported as reproduced independently (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, NIST, PTB, SYRTE and others, several species).

Every member's case against B048 centres on the same reservations: distinctness from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, the claims of other lattice-clock contributors (Lemonde, Takamoto and others), and timing relative to the redefinition of the second.

Lindroth, Eriksson, Olsson, Mehlig, Kroll and Pearce argue that 2005 recognised a frequency ruler and 2012 control of single quantum systems, whereas the lattice clock rests on a different mechanism (many neutral atoms at a magic wavelength); Eriksson, Mehlig, Kroll and Lindroth want any citation worded narrowly around the lattice clock.

Kroll, Lindroth, Olsson, Pearce and Mehlig say the pending SI redefinition should not by itself be a reason to wait; Johansson says it should be used neither as a reason to wait nor to act; Danielsson, Eriksson and Mehlig also list timing as an open question.

Johansson, Kroll, Lindroth, Olsson and Pearce say B054 (Higgs) is scientifically strong but that naming three people from ATLAS and CMS is hard to defend without a principled rule; these are stated positions, not votes.
scientific_disputes: Whether the lattice clock is a distinct physical achievement or a refinement of earlier precision-metrology work: every member names this as the strongest objection or an open question, and Eriksson adds that a purist could deny it is a new physical discovery. Johansson, Kroll and Eriksson point to many-body (spin-exchange) physics inside the clock as the argument that it is a physics result as well as a metrology advance.

Danielsson and Pearce keep B033 (IceCube) and B052 (EHT) as alternatives. Danielsson, Johansson and Mehlig note that the origin of the diffuse neutrino flux is unresolved and point-source evidence is at modest significance; Mehlig and Pearce note the EHT shadow-size gravity test is model dependent.
Kroll and Lindroth keep B025 (atom interferometry) and B021 (optical-lattice quantum simulation) as alternatives. Kroll declines to propose B025 as a second prize part.

B019 is an alternative for Eriksson, Johansson, Mehlig and Olsson, and members raise the 2016 topology prize as a possible overlap. Eriksson lists B036 (magic-angle graphene) as an alternative and concedes an open mechanism question and device-dependent reproducibility.

Mehlig now judges B011 (KPZ) unlikely this year. B001 (circuit QED) is Johansson's alternative but Eriksson, Mehlig and Olsson say the 2025 superconducting-circuits prize makes it hard to justify now.
attribution_disputes: B048: whether two names suffice given Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Boyd, Hollberg, the Yb and Hg groups and the ion-clock community. Mehlig says he would be more concerned if either Katori or Ye were dropped than about the split between them. Olsson says the record favours Katori on priority and asks for a check against the 2003 to 2005 papers. Danielsson says he cannot fully adjudicate the Katori and Ye relationship from the supplied text.

B054: the files carry different slates (Virdee for CMS in Danielsson's, Della Negra in Olsson's), and Johansson, Kroll, Lindroth and Pearce ask what principled rule could choose three names from four candidates across ATLAS and CMS.

B052 (Falcke, Zensus, Doeleman): Danielsson, Mehlig and Pearce note that imaging-algorithm and station leaders are left out. B033 (Halzen, Karle): Danielsson, Johansson and Pearce note that AMANDA, Baikal and other IceCube founders and leaders are not counted.

B019 (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp): Danielsson, Eriksson, Johansson, Lindroth, Mehlig and Olsson note that Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, Fu, Moore, Balents and others are not credited. B001: Eriksson, Lindroth and Mehlig note Girvin and Huang are not credited. B025: Lindroth notes Chu is not credited. B011: Lindroth and Mehlig note Parisi and the authors of the exact solutions are not credited.
maturity_disputes: Whether the pending redefinition of the second should affect the timing of B048: the files differ, with several members saying not to wait and Danielsson, Eriksson and Mehlig listing it as open. Kroll adds that waiting risks a missed or contested attribution as the field grows.
Relative maturity: Danielsson, Johansson and Mehlig describe B033 and B052 as strong but less complete than the clock, and Danielsson calls B033 a likely coming prize.
B001 and the 2025 prize: Eriksson, Mehlig and Olsson raise the closeness of the 2025 award; Johansson lists it as an open question that could count for or against.

All eight members say they are relying partly on memory or on colleagues' ballots for priority chronology and precision records, so claims about B048 maturity and credit are not yet checked against primary papers.
conflict_or_recusal_flags: Johansson: B001 (circuit QED) is the architecture of his own research and of the WACQT programme he directs, and its credited names are close colleagues. He flags a possible recusal issue for B001 and any configuration containing it. It does not touch the B048-only configuration.

Eriksson: chaired the 2025 committee that awarded the superconducting-circuit prize (relevant to B001). His DFT and spin-dynamics work for MAX IV and ESS is a general field connection to B019 and B036, not a tie to a named candidate.

Kroll: spent a year in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, and Ye is associated with that environment at JILA; he reports no joint work or financial tie to Ye or Katori. His WACQT role overlaps institutionally with Chalmers (relevant to B001, not B048).

Olsson: Fellow of the University of Tokyo since 2025, and Katori is Tokyo-based; no known collaboration with Katori or Ye. She regards this as disclosure only, not recusal, and says she will follow the chair's view.

Lindroth: long-time collaborator of Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and co-author with the Lund and Ursula Keller groups; none is credited in any shortlisted candidate, and she sees no need for recusal.

Mehlig shares a Gothenburg physics environment with Johansson and Olsson (Chalmers) but reports no collaboration with a credited name. Danielsson reports no specific conflict. Pearce (chair) reports no tie to Katori, Ye, Halzen, Karle or the EHT leaders, but notes that IceCube and EHT lie close to his own astroparticle field.
questions_for_round2: Is the lattice clock distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, and what citation wording makes that clear? Should it name only the lattice clock, and should it mention many-body physics or the 10^-18 level?

Is the chronology firm: Katori's 2003 magic-wavelength proposal and early strontium lattice clocks, versus Ye's record accuracy and many-body work? Which atomic-physics members (Lindroth, Kroll, Johansson, Olsson) can state it from primary papers, and does it change the credit split?
Do Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Boyd, Hollberg or anyone else have a claim strong enough to displace or join Katori and Ye, given the limit of three laureates? If so, on what documented ground?
Should the pending redefinition of the second affect timing in either direction, and do Danielsson, Eriksson and Mehlig, who list it as open, hold that position or join those who say not to wait?

Is a second prize part worth considering at all? Pearce raises it, Kroll declines B025 as a second part, and Lindroth notes a combination with B048 would need five names. If a second part is considered, which candidate has a credit set that can be defended within three names in total?

For the alternatives that members have raised (B019, B033, B052, B054, B025, B021, B036, B001, B011), is there a credit set that the members who raised the concerns would accept: a principled rule for B054, an answer on Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang for B019, and an answer on Girvin and Huang for B001?

How should the disclosed flags (Johansson on B001, Eriksson as 2025 chair, Olsson's Tokyo fellowship, Kroll's Boulder history) be recorded, and does any require recusal if the relevant candidate returns in the final ballot?
summary.chair_observation: In round 1 all eight files explicitly prefer a single-part B048 configuration crediting Katori and Ye, and several members say they moved there from a different opening first choice. The reservations (distinctness from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, other lattice-clock contributors, timing around the redefinition of the second) appear in every file and are offered mostly as judgements. Round 2 should test the chronology and credit claims that members are taking from memory, and check whether any alternative has a defensible credit set, before treating the convergence as settled.
